title: Masses, springs and modes
facts_to_cover: Why it vibrates: The spring tends to return to **equilibrium**, and a moving mass tends to **keep moving**, so the mass overshoots and the cycle repeats.
Mass and stiffness: **More mass lowers the frequency, and more stiffness raises the frequency.**
Directions: **Longitudinal** motion (back and forth along the spring) and **transverse** motion (up and down) behave the same way.
Mode: A **mode** is one way a system can vibrate. **N masses give N modes.**
Higher modes: The more the masses move **against each other**, the more the springs stretch and compress, so the mode has more stiffness and a **higher frequency**.
Local rule: **A mass changes the frequency only where it moves, and a spring changes the frequency only where it stretches.**
Infinitely many: An infinite number of masses and springs along a line is a **string**. Spread over a surface, it is a **membrane**, such as a drum or the vocal folds.

current_blocks.main: **A mass-spring system is a mass attached to a spring, and it can vibrate in two directions.** In longitudinal motion the mass moves back and forth along the spring, and in transverse motion it moves up and down across it.
current_blocks.sub: In both directions, the spring pulls the mass back toward equilibrium, the position where the spring is neither stretched nor compressed. The moving mass keeps going past equilibrium, so it overshoots, and the spring pulls it back again.
current_blocks.end: So longitudinal and transverse vibration work the same way. Only the direction of the motion is different.

current_blocks.main: **More mass lowers the frequency, and more stiffness raises the frequency, if nothing else changes.**
current_blocks.sub: More mass is harder to get moving and to turn around, so each cycle takes longer. A stiffer spring pulls back harder, so the mass returns faster.
current_blocks.end: When you predict a change, say what changed and what stayed the same, because mass and stiffness push the frequency in opposite directions.

current_blocks.main: **Two masses joined by springs have two modes.** In Mode 1 they move together, and in Mode 2 they move in opposite directions.
current_blocks.sub: When they move together, the middle spring hardly stretches. When they move in opposite directions, the middle spring stretches a lot, which adds stiffness and raises the frequency.
current_blocks.end: A mode is a pattern of the whole system. Both masses take part in each mode.

current_blocks.main: **Three masses have three modes.** In Mode 1 all three move together, in Mode 2 the middle mass stays still, and in Mode 3 each mass moves opposite to its neighbor.
current_blocks.sub: In Mode 2 the two outer masses move in opposite directions, so the middle one does not move. In Mode 3 the springs stretch the most, so Mode 3 has the highest frequency.
current_blocks.end: Extra mass on the middle mass lowers Mode 1 and Mode 3, where it moves, but does not change Mode 2, where it is still.

current_blocks.main: **N masses give N modes.** Each new mass that can move on its own adds one more way for the system to vibrate.
current_blocks.sub: Lower modes have big, broad movements, and higher modes switch direction more often along the system. The system can vibrate in several modes at once.
current_blocks.end: With an infinite number of masses and springs, you get a string, which has a whole series of modes.

An infinite number of masses and springs along a line is a **string**. Spread over a surface, it is a **membrane**, such as a drum or the vocal folds.

questions.q: Why do multiple mass systems have multiple frequencies?
questions.a: A system with several masses can vibrate in several ways, called modes, because the masses can move together or against each other. When the masses move against each other, the springs between them stretch and compress more, so more stiffness is working and that mode vibrates faster. Each mode therefore has its own frequency, and a system with N masses has N modes and N frequencies.

questions.q: How many modes does a 3-mass system have?
questions.a: A 3-mass system has three modes, because a system with N masses has N modes of vibration.

questions.q: Four masses are joined by springs between two walls. How many modes does the system have, and what are the masses doing in the lowest and highest modes?
questions.a: The system has four modes, one for each mass. In the lowest mode, Mode 1, all four masses move in the same direction at the same time. In the highest mode, Mode 4, every mass moves opposite to its neighbors, so every spring is stretched and compressed and the frequency is highest.

questions.q: Which mode of the 3-mass system has the highest frequency? Why?
questions.a: Mode 3 has the highest frequency. In Mode 3 the middle mass moves opposite to the two outer masses, so every spring is stretched and compressed as much as possible. That puts the most stiffness to work, and more stiffness makes the system vibrate faster.

questions.q: Which mode of a 2-mass system has the lowest frequency, and why?
questions.a: Mode 1 has the lowest frequency. In Mode 1 the two masses move together, so the middle spring is carried along without stretching. Only the two outer springs are working, so Mode 1 has less stiffness than Mode 2 and vibrates more slowly.

questions.q: If you increase mass 2, what happens to the frequencies of each of the modes?
questions.a: Mode 1 and Mode 3 go down, and Mode 2 stays the same. The middle mass moves in Mode 1 and in Mode 3, so making it heavier slows those modes. In Mode 2 the middle mass does not move, and a mass that does not move has no effect on the frequency.

questions.q: In the 3-mass system, what happens to each mode if you make mass 1 (an outer mass) heavier?
questions.a: All three modes go down. The outer mass moves in Mode 1, Mode 2 and Mode 3, and a heavier mass that is moving lowers the frequency. No mode leaves an outer mass still, so none of the three frequencies stays the same.

questions.q: In a 2-mass system, what happens to each mode if you make the middle spring stiffer?
questions.a: Mode 1 stays the same and Mode 2 goes up. In Mode 1 the masses move together, so the middle spring is never stretched and its extra stiffness does nothing. In Mode 2 the masses move against each other, so the middle spring is stretched and compressed and the extra stiffness raises the frequency.

questions.q: What do you get when you have an infinite number of masses and springs?
questions.a: You get a string, like a guitar or piano string. Every small piece of a string has mass, and every small piece stretches like a spring, so a string vibrates in modes like a chain of masses, only with infinitely many of them. Spread over a surface instead of a line, the same idea gives a membrane such as a drum or the vocal folds.

questions.q: What happens to the frequency of a single mass on a spring if you make the spring stiffer? If you make the mass heavier?
questions.a: A stiffer spring raises the frequency, because it pulls the mass back toward equilibrium with more force and turns it around sooner. A heavier mass lowers the frequency, because a heavier mass is harder to start and stop, so each back-and-forth cycle takes longer.

title: Where the springiness is, and what a local change does
facts_to_cover: Alternation: **Where a vibrating system moves the most, it stretches the least, and where it does not move, it stretches the most.**
Shortcut: The springiest locations are the points of **no movement**, which are the fixed ends and the points where the mode crosses its resting line.
Ends: A **fixed end is always springy**, and a **free end is always moving**, in every mode.
Added mass: Extra mass lowers a mode's frequency **only where that mode is moving**.
Added stiffness: Extra stiffness raises a mode's frequency **only where that mode is stretching**.
Both at once: Adding mass and stiffness together does **not** cancel out, except for a single mass on a single spring, because at one spot in one mode only one of the two matters.

Perturbation theory: It predicts how a small change in one location affects vibration. In the late nineteenth century, wax placed where a drum vibrated a lot lowered its pitch, and wax placed where it did not vibrate had no effect.

current_blocks.main: **In a vibrating system such as a string or a chain of masses, a change at one spot affects each mode depending on what that spot is doing in that mode.** Extra mass matters where the mode is moving, and extra stiffness matters where it is stretching.
current_blocks.sub: Where a mode moves the most, extra mass wins and the frequency goes down. Where it does not move, it stretches the most, so extra stiffness wins and the frequency goes up.
current_blocks.end: The same spot can be still in one mode and moving in another, so adding mass and stiffness together can raise one mode and lower another. They do not cancel out.

questions.q: This is Mode 5 of a string fixed at both ends. Circle the areas where there is the most springiness.
questions.a: Circle the two fixed ends and the four points where the string crosses its middle line, six places in all. At those points the string does not move, but the pieces on either side move in opposite directions, so the string there is stretched and compressed the most. The tops of the five bumps have the most motion and the least springiness.

questions.q: This is Mode 3 of a string fixed at both ends. Where is the most springiness, and where is the most motion?
questions.a: The most springiness is at the two fixed ends and at the two points where the string crosses its middle line, four places in all, because the string does not move there. The most motion is at the tops of the three bumps, where the string swings the most and is hardly stretched.

questions.q: This picture shows Mode 4 of a building. Circle the areas where there is the most springiness.
questions.a: Circle the fixed base and the three points where the building crosses its resting position, four places in all. Those points do not move, but the parts above and below them move in opposite directions, so the structure there stretches and compresses the most. The free top moves the most and is the least springy, so it is not circled.

questions.q: This diagram shows Mode 2 of a building. Where is the most springiness?
questions.a: The most springiness is at the fixed base and at the one point above it where the building crosses its resting position. Those two points do not move, so the structure there is stretched and compressed the most. The free top moves the most and is the least springy.

questions.q: If we increase the stiffness and mass of the string at the boxed location (where Mode 3 crosses its middle line and Mode 4 is at the top of a bump), what happens to Mode 3 and Mode 4's frequencies, and why?
questions.a: Mode 3 goes up and Mode 4 goes down. In Mode 3 the boxed spot does not move but is stretched the most, so the added mass does nothing and the added stiffness raises the frequency. In Mode 4 the boxed spot moves the most and is not stretched, so the added mass lowers the frequency and the added stiffness does nothing.

questions.q: The box is moved to a spot where Mode 3 is at the top of a bump and Mode 4 crosses its middle line. Mass and stiffness are added there. What happens?
questions.a: Now Mode 3 goes down and Mode 4 goes up. In Mode 3 the spot moves the most and is hardly stretched, so the added mass lowers the frequency. In Mode 4 the spot does not move but is stretched the most, so the added stiffness raises the frequency.

questions.q: If we increase the mass and stiffness of the building at its very top, what happens to the frequency of Mode 4, and why?
questions.a: The frequency of Mode 4 goes down. The top of the building is the free end, so in every mode it moves the most and is hardly stretched. The added mass matters there and lowers the frequency, while the added stiffness does nothing because nothing is stretching at the top.

questions.q: If we increase the mass and stiffness of the building at its very base, what happens to the frequency of Mode 4, and why?
questions.a: The frequency of Mode 4 goes up. The base is the fixed end, so it never moves but is always stretched and compressed. The added mass does nothing there because the base does not move, while the added stiffness raises the frequency.

questions.q: In Mode 3 of a string fixed at both ends, point B does not move and point C is at the bottom of a bump. What happens to Mode 3 if you add a small weight at B? At C? If you stiffen the string at B?
questions.a: A weight at B leaves Mode 3 the same, because B does not move in Mode 3. A weight at C lowers Mode 3's frequency, because C swings the most and the extra mass counts there. Stiffening the string at B raises Mode 3's frequency, because B is where the string stretches the most.

questions.q: The same spot B is moving in Mode 1. Does a weight at B change Mode 1's frequency?
questions.a: Yes, the weight lowers Mode 1's frequency. In Mode 1 the whole string is one bump, so the spot at B is moving, and extra mass at a moving spot slows the vibration.

title: Harmonics and formants: fixed-fixed and fixed-free systems
facts_to_cover: Fixed-fixed: A system fixed at both ends, such as a string or the **vocal folds**, has modes at **1, 2, 3, 4 times** the first. These are **harmonics**.
Why whole numbers: The first mode is **half a wave**, and each higher mode must fit a whole number of those half-waves between the two fixed ends. Mode N contains N copies of Mode 1.
Fixed-free: A system fixed at one end and free at the other, such as a **building** or the **air in the vocal tract**, has modes at **1, 3, 5, 7 times** the first. These are **formants**.

Why odd numbers: The first mode is a **quarter-wave packet** from no motion to the most motion. The free end must always be moving, so packets are added two at a time, giving one, three, five and seven packets.
Spacing: Fixed-fixed modes are spaced by the first frequency. Fixed-free modes are spaced by **twice** the first frequency.
Building analogy: A building is fixed to the ground and free at the top, just as the air in the vocal tract is fixed at the closed vocal folds and free at the open lips.
Spectrum: A **spectrum** has frequency on the horizontal axis and amplitude on the vertical axis, with one spike for each mode that is present.
Scientific method: The theory that the vocal folds are a membrane predicts **equidistant harmonics** (evenly spaced harmonics). Recordings in Praat confirmed the prediction.

questions.q: A string is fixed on both sides. If Mode 1 has frequency 200 Hz, what frequency does Mode 5 have?
questions.a: Mode 5 has a frequency of 1000 Hz. In a string fixed at both ends, each mode is a whole-number multiple of the first, and Mode 5 contains five copies of Mode 1, so it is five times 200 Hz.

questions.q: A string fixed at both ends has Mode 1 at 150 Hz. What are Modes 2 and 3? If one end is freed and Mode 1 stays at 150 Hz, what are Modes 2 and 3 now?
questions.a: Fixed at both ends, Modes 2 and 3 are 300 and 450 Hz, which are two and three times 150. Fixed at one end and free at the other, Modes 2 and 3 are 450 and 750 Hz, which are three and five times 150, because only the odd multiples occur. The fixed-fixed modes are 150 Hz apart, and the fixed-free modes are 300 Hz apart.

questions.q: Why are the frequencies of fixed-fixed vibratory systems spaced the way they are?
questions.a: In a system fixed at both ends, the first mode is half a wave, going from no motion at one end to the most motion in the middle and back to no motion. Every higher mode must fit a whole number of those half-waves into the same length, because both ends must stay still. Mode 2 fits two, so it vibrates twice as fast, and Mode 3 fits three, so the frequencies are evenly spaced whole-number multiples of the first.

questions.q: Why are the formants of a fixed-free system 1, 3, 5, etc. multiples of the base frequency?
questions.a: In a fixed-free system the basic piece is a quarter-wave packet, which runs from no motion at the fixed end to the most motion at the free end. Every mode must start still at the fixed end and end with the most motion at the free end. One extra packet would leave a still point at the free end, which cannot happen, so packets are added two at a time, giving one, three, five and seven packets and odd-multiple frequencies.

questions.q: If F1 is 500 Hz, what are F2 and F3?
questions.a: F2 is 1500 Hz and F3 is 2500 Hz. The air in the vocal tract is a fixed-free system, so its formants are odd multiples of the first, which are three times and five times 500 Hz, not two and three times.

questions.q: What aspect of speech has the properties in the fixed-free question?
questions.a: The formants of the air in the vocal tract have these properties. The air is fixed at the closed vocal folds and free at the open lips, so its frequencies of vibration, the formants, are odd multiples of the first formant.

questions.q: What aspect of speech has frequencies at whole-number multiples, and why?
questions.a: The harmonics of the vocal folds have whole-number multiples. The vocal folds are a membrane held in place along their edges, so they behave like a system fixed at both ends, and each mode is a whole number of copies of the first.

questions.q: What in speech is a building analogous to, and why does the analogy hold?
questions.a: A building is analogous to the air in the vocal tract. Both are fixed at one end and free at the other: the building is fixed to the ground and free at the top, and the air is fixed at the closed vocal folds and free at the open lips. Because the ends match, both have springiness at the fixed end, the most motion at the free end, and frequencies at odd multiples of the first.

questions.q: How is a building different from the air in the vocal tract?
questions.a: Engineers design a building to sway only in Mode 1, because higher modes would move floors in opposite directions and could break the structure. The air in the vocal tract vibrates in all of its modes at once, and speaking changes the mass and stiffness of the air at different locations to move those formants.

questions.q: Draw the spectrum for a string fixed at both ends with Mode 1 at 200 Hz, up to Mode 6.
questions.a: Draw frequency along the horizontal axis and amplitude up the vertical axis. Put six evenly spaced spikes at 200, 400, 600, 800, 1000 and 1200 Hz, one for each mode. If the modes are equally strong, the spikes can be drawn the same height.

questions.q: Draw the spectrum for a fixed-free system with Mode 1 at 200 Hz, up to Mode 4.
questions.a: Draw spikes only at the odd multiples: 200, 600, 1000 and 1400 Hz. A fixed-free system has no even multiples, because an even number of quarter-wave packets would leave a still point at the free end.

questions.q: If the vocal folds have their base frequency, F0, at 150 Hz, draw the spectrum for the first 5 harmonics.
questions.a: Draw spikes at 150, 300, 450, 600 and 750 Hz, with frequency along the bottom and amplitude going up. The vocal folds are a membrane fixed along its edges, so their harmonics are whole-number multiples of F0 and the spikes are evenly spaced 150 Hz apart.

title: The vocal tract, constrictions and the vowels /i/, /a/ and /u/
facts_to_cover: Fixed-free tube: The air in the vocal tract is **fixed at the glottis** (closed vocal folds, so the air can only be compressed) and **free at the lips** (the air moves in and out).
Schwa: With no constriction, as in **done**, the formants are about **500, 1500 and 2500 Hz**.
Constriction: A **constriction** (narrowing) packs the air into a smaller space, which makes it both **heavier** (denser) and **stiffer**.

Four steps: Find the location, decide whether the air there is mostly **moving** or mostly **compressed** in that mode, pick the extra that counts (mass if moving, stiffness if compressed), then say whether the formant goes **down** or **up**.
/u/ (dune): The constriction is at the lips, where the air is moving in both modes, so **F1 and F2 both go down**.
/i/ (dean): The constriction is two-thirds of the way from the glottis. The air there moves in Mode 1 and is compressed in Mode 2, so **F1 goes down and F2 goes up** (the formants move apart).
/a/ (Don): The constriction is one-third of the way from the glottis. The air there is compressed in Mode 1 and moves in Mode 2, so **F1 goes up and F2 goes down** (the formants move together).
Reasoning backward: A large rise means the air there was springy and hardly moving. A large fall means the air there was moving a lot.

current_blocks.end: The location of the constriction changes the formants, so the same voice from the vocal folds can make different vowels.

current_blocks.sub: Where the air is mostly moving, the extra mass wins and the formant goes down. Where the air is mostly compressed, the extra stiffness wins and the formant goes up.
current_blocks.end: So a big rise in a formant means the air there was compressed and hardly moving in that mode, and a big fall means it was moving a lot.

With no constriction, as in **done**, the formants are about **500, 1500 and 2500 Hz**. This neutral vowel is schwa.

To work out what a constriction does, find its location, decide whether the air there is mostly **moving** or mostly **compressed** in that mode, pick the extra that counts (mass if moving, stiffness if compressed), and then say whether the formant goes **down** or **up**.

questions.q: If I constrict the vocal tract somewhere and I raise the formant a great deal, what must be true of air motion versus springiness at this location?
questions.a: At that location the air must be very springy and hardly moving in that mode. A constriction adds both mass and stiffness, and the formant went up, so the added stiffness is what counted. Stiffness only counts where the air is compressed and expanded, and the added mass did nothing because the air there was not moving.

questions.q: If I constrict the vocal tract somewhere and I lower the formant a great deal, what must be true at this location?
questions.a: At that location the air must be moving a lot and hardly compressed in that mode. The formant went down, so the added mass is what counted, and mass only counts where the air is moving. This is what happens at the lips for /u/.

questions.q: A classmate says more mass lowers the frequency and more stiffness raises it, so a constriction always cancels out. What is wrong with this argument?
questions.a: In any one mode, at most locations only one of the two changes matters. If the air at the constriction is mostly moving, it is not being compressed, so only the extra mass counts and the formant goes down. If the air there is mostly compressed, it is not moving, so only the extra stiffness counts and the formant goes up, which is why the same constriction can push F1 and F2 in opposite directions.

questions.q: Why is the air in the vocal tract a fixed-free system? Say which end is which.
questions.a: The glottis end is closed off by the vocal folds, so the air there cannot move and can only be compressed and expanded, which makes it the fixed end. The lip end is open, so the air there moves freely in and out without being compressed against anything, which makes it the free end.

questions.q: Compared with done, what happens to F1 and F2 in dune, and why?
questions.a: Both F1 and F2 go down. Lip rounding creates a constriction at the free end, where the air moves the most in every mode. The added mass therefore counts in both Mode 1 and Mode 2, and extra mass at a moving location lowers the frequency.

questions.q: Compared with done, what happens to F1 and F2 in dean, and why?
questions.a: F1 goes down and F2 goes up. The constriction is about two-thirds of the way from the glottis. In Mode 1 the air there is moving, so the added mass lowers F1, and in Mode 2 the air there is compressed, so the added stiffness raises F2.

questions.q: Compared with done, what happens to F1 and F2 in Don, and why?
questions.a: F1 goes up and F2 goes down. The constriction is about one-third of the way from the glottis. In Mode 1 the air there is compressed, so the added stiffness raises F1, and in Mode 2 the air there is moving, so the added mass lowers F2.

questions.q: A new constriction is placed deep in the throat, one-fifth of the way from the glottis, where the air is compressed in both Mode 1 and Mode 2. What happens to F1 and F2?
questions.a: Both F1 and F2 go up. The location is near the fixed end, where the air is compressed in both modes, so the added stiffness is what counts in both, and extra stiffness raises the frequency.

questions.q: Why does rounding the lips lower every formant?
questions.a: The lips are the free end of the vocal tract, and the free end is a location of maximum motion in every mode. A constriction there adds mass where the air is moving, so it lowers every formant. This is the same reason that adding mass at the top of a building lowers every mode.

title: Source and filter, and F0
facts_to_cover: Source: The **vocal folds** are the source. They produce **harmonics** at whole-number multiples of **F0**, the base frequency.
Filter: The **air in the vocal tract** is the filter. Its **formants** decide which harmonics are loud.
Core rule: **A formant makes the harmonics closest to it louder, and harmonics far from any formant come out weaker.** The outline of the harmonic heights is the **envelope**.
Vowels: The harmonics stay the same from vowel to vowel. Only their heights change, and the envelope is what makes each vowel distinct.
F0: Heavy, loose vocal folds give a low F0. Tight, light vocal folds give a high F0, so the harmonics are spaced farther apart.
High voices: With a high F0, few harmonics fall near each formant, so the formants are hard to see. This is why a toddler's or a soprano's vowels are hard to identify.
F0 carries meaning: F0 falls at the end of a statement and rises at the end of a question, and it signals sarcasm or pretending.

current_blocks.main: **The vocal folds are the source.** They make harmonics at whole-number multiples of F0.
current_blocks.sub: A higher F0 spreads the harmonics farther apart. Tighter, lighter vocal folds raise F0, and heavier, looser vocal folds lower it.
current_blocks.end: With an F0 of 150 Hz, the first five harmonics are 150, 300, 450, 600 and 750 Hz.

current_blocks.main: **The vocal tract is the filter.** It makes the harmonics near its formants louder and the ones far from its formants weaker. F1 and F2 are the first two formants.
current_blocks.sub: The outline of the harmonic heights is the envelope, and its peaks show the formants.
current_blocks.end: Changing the vowel moves the formants while F0 stays the same, and changing F0 changes the spacing of the harmonics while the vowel stays the same. So pitch and vowel are separate.

current_blocks.main: **A high F0 spreads the harmonics far apart, so few of them fall near each formant.**
current_blocks.sub: A low voice has many harmonics close together near each formant, which shows the envelope clearly. A high voice has few, so the envelope is hard to see.
current_blocks.end: That is why a soprano's or a toddler's vowels are hard to identify. The vocal tract still has its formants; there just are not enough harmonics near them.

questions.q: What does the source supply and what does the filter do in speech?
questions.a: The vocal folds are the source, and they supply the harmonics, which are whole-number multiples of F0. The air in the vocal tract is the filter, and its formants make the harmonics near them louder and the ones far from them weaker. So the source decides which frequencies are present, and the filter decides which of them are loud.

questions.q: Two vowels are said at the same pitch. What is the same and what is different in their spectra?
questions.a: The harmonics are the same, because the vocal folds vibrate at the same F0 for both vowels. The heights of the harmonics are different, because each vowel has its constriction in a different place, which moves the formants and changes the envelope.

questions.q: Why are a toddler's vowels hard to identify?
questions.a: A toddler has a very high F0, so the harmonics are spaced far apart. Few harmonics fall near each formant, and a formant can fall between two harmonics, so the envelope is hard to see. The formants are still there, but there are too few harmonics to reveal them.

questions.q: If the vocal folds become tighter, what happens to F0 and to the spacing of the harmonics?
questions.a: F0 goes up, because tighter vocal folds are stiffer, and more stiffness raises the frequency. The harmonics are multiples of F0, so they are spaced farther apart.

title: Spectra, spectrograms and speech over time
facts_to_cover: Spectrum: A **spectrum** shows one instant, with frequency on the horizontal axis and amplitude on the vertical axis.
Spectrogram: A **spectrogram** lines up many spectra over time. Time is on the horizontal axis, frequency on the vertical axis, and **darkness** shows amplitude.
Dark bands: The **dark bands are the formants**. F1 is the lowest band and F2 is the next one up.
Transitions: From schwa to /i/, the bands move apart. From schwa to /u/, both drop. From schwa to /a/, they move together.
Where were you a year ago?: The formants never stay still, because every sound moves the constriction. Speech is a continuous series of constrictions, not a list of separate vowels.
ma and na: When the m of ma is joined to the a of na, listeners hear na. Listeners decide on the consonant during the vowel, after the consonant is over (Malécot, 1950s).

current_blocks.main: **A spectrum shows one moment, and a spectrogram shows many moments in a row.** In a spectrogram, time is on the horizontal axis and frequency is on the vertical axis.
current_blocks.sub: Darkness shows amplitude, so the darkest bands are the formants. The bands rise and fall as the vocal tract changes shape.
current_blocks.end: Going from /i/ to /a/, F1 rises and F2 falls.

current_blocks.main: **In connected speech the formants keep changing, because the tongue and lips keep moving from one sound to the next, as in "Where were you a year ago?"**
current_blocks.sub: F2 rises when the tongue moves toward /i/, and the formants drop when the lips round toward /u/.
current_blocks.end: So the direction the bands move carries information about the sounds, not just the middle of each vowel.

current_blocks.main: **A consonant is identified partly from the vowel after it.** When the m of ma is joined to the a of na, listeners hear na.
current_blocks.sub: The vowel from na still has the formant transition that came from the n, and listeners use that transition.
current_blocks.end: So listeners decide on the consonant during the vowel, after the consonant is over. Speech is heard as a sequence, not one slice at a time.

items: **From schwa to /i/, the bands move apart.** From schwa to /u/, both drop. From schwa to /a/, they move together.

questions.q: Describe a spectrogram.
questions.a: A spectrogram lines up many spectra side by side over time. Time runs along the horizontal axis and frequency runs up the vertical axis, and the darkness of each spot shows how much amplitude there is at that frequency and time. The formants appear as dark bands, so you can follow them as they rise and fall, for example F1 rising and F2 falling from /i/ to /a/.

questions.q: How is a spectrum different from a spectrogram?
questions.a: A spectrum shows one frozen instant, with frequency on the horizontal axis and amplitude on the vertical axis. A spectrogram shows how the spectrum changes over time, with time on the horizontal axis, frequency on the vertical axis and amplitude shown as darkness. Real speech is always changing, so a spectrogram shows the formants moving.

questions.q: A speaker starts on schwa and switches to another vowel. F1 goes down and F2 goes up. Which vowel? What if both go down?
questions.a: When F1 goes down and F2 goes up, the bands move apart, so the vowel is /i/ as in dean. When both F1 and F2 go down, the vowel is /u/ as in dune, because lip rounding lowers every formant.

questions.q: Describe the spectrogram of a speaker going from schwa to the vowel of Don.
questions.a: F1 goes up and F2 goes down, so the two lowest dark bands move toward each other. The constriction one-third of the way from the glottis is compressed in Mode 1 and moving in Mode 2, so it raises F1 and lowers F2.

questions.q: Why do listeners hear na when the m of ma is joined to the a of na?
questions.a: The information about the consonant is carried mostly by the vowel that follows it. After n, one formant of the vowel drops, and after m, that formant stays flat, so the a from na still signals n. Listeners therefore decide which consonant they heard during the vowel, after the consonant is over.

title: Neural networks: inner products, weights and decisions
facts_to_cover: Task: The vowel network takes **F1 and F2** and decides among five words, **done, dune, dean, Don and Dan**.
Knowledge: **The network's knowledge is stored in its weights**, which are positive or negative numbers.
Inner product: Each neuron multiplies each incoming activation by its weight and adds the results. This **inner product** is the core calculation of all AI.
Forward propagation: The inner products are carried layer by layer from the input to the output.
Output: The output is a **probability distribution**, numbers between 0 and 1 that **add up to 1**. The largest one is the decision.
Desired output: The right answer is a **one-hot** list, 1 for the correct word and 0 everywhere else, such as 0, 0, 1, 0, 0 for dean.
Direction questions: A positive activation times a positive weight is positive, so raising either one pushes that output's probability **up**. A negative weight would push it down.
page_tags: Lecture 14 · p24 · Lecture 15 · p3 · Lecture 16 · p3

current_blocks.main: **The vowel network takes F1 and F2 as its two inputs and gives a probability for each of five words, done, dune, dean, Don and Dan.**
current_blocks.sub: The hidden layers turn the two formants into new numbers for the output layer, and the weights decide which formant patterns point to which word.
current_blocks.end: A low F1 and a high F2 is /i/, so the right answer for that input is dean.

current_blocks.main: **A weight decides how much an incoming activation counts for the next neuron.** The neuron multiplies each input by its weight and adds the results, which is the inner product.
current_blocks.sub: A positive weight keeps the input's sign, and a negative weight flips it. A bigger weight makes that input count more.
current_blocks.end: The weights start out random and become useful through learning.

current_blocks.ref: Lecture 14 · p24 · Lecture 15 · p3 · Lecture 16 · p3
current_blocks.main: **Forward propagation makes a guess using the current weights.** Each layer takes the activations from the layer before and passes its results to the next.
current_blocks.sub: The input layer only supplies F1 and F2, and the output layer gives the probabilities for the five words.
current_blocks.end: A forward pass can run correctly and still give the wrong answer, because the weights may not be learned yet.

current_blocks.main: **A probability distribution has numbers between 0 and 1 that add up to 1.** Each number is the chance for one word.
current_blocks.sub: The desired output puts 1 on the correct word and 0 on the rest, such as 0, 0, 1, 0, 0 for dean.
current_blocks.end: A guess can add up to 1 and still put the most probability on the wrong word. Being valid and being correct are different.

current_blocks.main: **To decide whether a weight should go up, look at the activation coming in and at whether that output should go up or down.** With a positive activation, raising the weight raises that output.
current_blocks.sub: If that output is already too high, raising the weight makes the error worse. For an early weight, the effect also depends on all the weights after it.
current_blocks.end: So you cannot just say every weight should go up. You have to follow its effect to the error.

items: **The network's knowledge is stored in its weights, which are positive or negative numbers.**
Each neuron multiplies each incoming activation by its weight and adds the results. This **inner product** is the core calculation of all AI.

questions.q: If an activation of 1.57 feeds the done output through a weight of positive 0.1, what happens to the probability of done if the weight goes up? If the activation goes up?
questions.a: The probability of done goes up in both cases. The contribution to the done output is the activation times the weight, and both are positive, so raising either one makes the product larger and pushes done up. No multiplication is needed, only the signs.

questions.q: What happens to the probability of done if that same weight were negative and the activation went up?
questions.a: The probability of done goes down. A positive activation times a negative weight is negative, so a larger activation makes the contribution more negative and pushes the done output down.

questions.q: Is 0.2, 0.3, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3 a valid probability distribution?
questions.a: No. The numbers add up to 1.1, and a probability distribution must add up to exactly 1.

questions.q: The first of five categories is correct. Write the desired output.
questions.a: The desired output is 1, 0, 0, 0, 0. It puts all of the probability on the correct category and zero on every other category.

questions.q: The desired output over done, dune, dean, Don, Dan is 0, 0, 0, 1, 0, and the network outputs 0.10, 0.15, 0.60, 0.10, 0.05. Which vowel was said, which did the network guess, and what is the loss?
questions.a: Don was said, and the network guessed dean, because dean has the largest probability, 0.60. The loss is a number that measures how far the computed output is from the desired output, for example how much probability it put on dean where there should be a 0.

questions.q: What does Linear mean in the network code?
questions.a: Linear means the layer computes inner products. Each neuron multiplies each incoming number by its weight and adds the results, with no other step.

title: Backpropagation: why learning starts at the end
facts_to_cover: Learning: Every network starts with **random weights** and learns by correcting its mistakes, one small step at a time.
Order: **The last set of weights is updated first, and the first set of weights is updated last.**
Why the end is easy: The last weights affect the output probabilities **directly**, so one inner product shows whether each should go up or down.

Why the start is hard: A first-layer weight affects the first hidden layer, which affects the next layer and the next, so its effect on the decision passes through every layer and depends on all the later weights.
Dynamic programming: Solve the easy problem first and reuse its answer for the bigger problem that contains it (Bellman and Viterbi).
Formula: **Backpropagation is stochastic gradient descent plus dynamic programming.** SGD changes each weight a little, and dynamic programming sets the order.
Credit: Backpropagation was worked out in the mid-1980s, and Geoffrey Hinton won the 2024 Nobel Prize in Physics for it.

current_blocks.main: **Backpropagation is how a neural network learns its weights from its mistakes, and it starts at the output.** The last weights are directly connected to the error, while an early weight affects the output only through every later layer.
current_blocks.sub: Working out the last layer first and reusing that answer for the earlier layers is dynamic programming.
current_blocks.end: Backpropagation works out how each weight should change, and SGD then changes each weight a little. Backpropagation is SGD plus dynamic programming.

items: **Every network starts with random weights and learns by correcting its mistakes, one small step at a time.**
**The last set of weights is updated first, and the first set of weights is updated last.**
Backpropagation was worked out in the mid-1980s, and Geoffrey Hinton won the 2024 Nobel Prize in Physics for it.

questions.q: In what order are the weights updated?
questions.a: The last set of weights is updated first, and the first set of weights is updated last. Each layer's update reuses what was already worked out for the layers after it.

questions.q: Why does backpropagation start at the end?
questions.a: The last set of weights affects the output probabilities, which are the decision, directly, so it is easy to tell whether raising or lowering each one makes the loss go up or down. A weight from the input to the first hidden layer affects the first hidden layer, then the second, then the third, and only then the output, so working out how to change it is a very complex problem that contains the problem of changing the last weights. Following dynamic programming, the simplest problem is solved first, and its answer makes the harder problems easier until the most complex one is solved.

questions.q: What two methods together train the network's weights?
questions.a: Stochastic gradient descent and backpropagation. Backpropagation works backward from the error to find which way each weight should change, and stochastic gradient descent moves each weight a small step in that direction.

questions.q: Backpropagation is made of what two parts?
questions.a: Backpropagation is stochastic gradient descent plus dynamic programming. Stochastic gradient descent nudges each weight a small step in the direction that lowers the error, and dynamic programming sets the order, from the last weights back to the first.

questions.q: Which part of training is the SGD part, and which is the dynamic programming part? What are the small problem and the big problem?
questions.a: The SGD part is the adjusting, where each weight takes a small step, sized by the learning rate, in the direction that lowers the error. The dynamic programming part is the order of assigning blame, last layer first, reusing each layer's blame for the layer before it. The small problem is the blame of the last layer's weights, and the big problem is the blame of the early weights.

questions.q: The network said done but the answer was dean. Should a last weight that pushes done up go up or down? Why?
questions.a: It should go down. The probability of done is too high, because the desired output for done is zero. Lowering a weight that pushes done up shrinks its contribution and pulls the probability of done toward zero.

questions.q: If the network already makes the right decision on a recording, what does it learn from it?
questions.a: It learns nothing from that recording, because there is no error to correct. This can be a problem, because a network can keep getting the right answers by memorizing its data without learning the pattern underneath.

title: Reading the PyTorch code
facts_to_cover: Import lines: They bring in the **torch library**, which already contains the programs for inner products and backpropagation, so none of it has to be written by hand.
Sequential: The network is **a sequence of layers, one after another**.
nn.Linear(2, 3): A processing layer that **takes input from 2 neurons and has 3 neurons**. It computes inner products.
Counting layers: The **input layer gets no line**, because it does no processing. The **last line is always the output layer**. nn.Sigmoid lines are not layers.
Matching: The first number on each line must equal the second number on the line before it.
Training lines: **SGD** is stochastic gradient descent, **lr** is the learning rate, **loss** is the mistake, **backward** runs backpropagation and **step** updates the weights.
Learning rate: **A higher learning rate learns faster but less accurately. A lower one learns more accurately but more slowly.**

questions.q: What do the import lines do, and what does Sequential mean?
questions.a: The import lines bring the torch library into Python, so the programs for inner products and backpropagation do not have to be written by hand. Sequential means the network is a sequence of layers, one after another, with each layer taking its input from the layer before it.

questions.q: What happens if the learning rate is raised from 0.1 to 0.3?
questions.a: The network learns faster, but its accuracy goes down. A larger learning rate takes bigger steps, so it approaches the answer quickly but keeps overshooting.

questions.q: Two learning curves differ only in learning rate. One rises fast and jumps around, and the other rises slowly and smoothly. Which used the larger learning rate?
questions.a: The one that rises fast and jumps around used the larger learning rate. Bigger steps get near the answer quickly but overshoot, while smaller steps are slower but smoother.

title: The sigmoid and where the idea came from
facts_to_cover: From the brain: **Lord Edgar Adrian** won the Nobel Prize in 1932 for showing that **neurons are nearly digital**, either firing or not firing.
What it does: The **sigmoid** takes an inner product and returns a number between 0 and 1.
Values: A large negative input gives about **0** (off), a large positive input gives about **1** (on), and an input of exactly 0 gives **0.5**.

Perception: Very different things can be perceived as the same (a friend with or without a hat), and very similar things as different (USC and UCLA), just like the flat parts and the steep middle of the sigmoid.
In code: nn.Sigmoid goes after each hidden layer. The last layer has no sigmoid, because its outputs go to the loss, which turns them into probabilities.
Bigger idea: Many basic ideas in AI, including neurons, inner products and near-digital firing, come from discoveries about real brains.

current_blocks.main: **The sigmoid turns an inner product into a number between 0 and 1.** A large negative input gives about 0, a large positive input gives about 1, and an input of 0 gives 0.5.
current_blocks.sub: The curve is steep in the middle and flat at both ends, so the same change in the input matters more near the middle.
current_blocks.end: Hidden sigmoid values are each between 0 and 1, but they do not have to add up to 1, so they are not a probability distribution.

current_blocks.main: **When the sigmoid changes a hidden value, every later layer changes too, because the next layer uses that value as its input.**
current_blocks.sub: Each hidden neuron first does its inner product and then applies the sigmoid, and the sigmoid's output is what goes to the next layer.
current_blocks.end: So the final probabilities can change even though F1 and F2 did not change.

questions.q: Where does the idea of the sigmoid come from?
questions.a: It comes from biology. Lord Edgar Adrian discovered that real neurons are nearly digital, firing or not firing, and won the Nobel Prize in 1932. The sigmoid copies this by squashing any inner product into a number between 0 and 1, so a neuron is nearly off or nearly on.

questions.q: A hidden neuron's inner product is minus 2. Is its sigmoid activation closer to 0 or 1, and what does that mean?
questions.a: It is closer to 0, because the input is negative. The neuron is mostly off and fires only rarely.

questions.q: If one input to that neuron goes up through a positive weight, what happens to its linear activation and its sigmoid activation?
questions.a: Both go up. The larger input times a positive weight raises the inner product, and the sigmoid always rises when its input rises, so the neuron fires more often.

questions.q: What is the sigmoid activation if the linear activation is exactly 0?
questions.a: It is 0.5, halfway between off and on, so the neuron is half active.

questions.q: How does the sigmoid match human perception?
questions.a: Some very different things are perceived as the same, and some very similar things are perceived as different. The flat parts of the sigmoid give the same output for very different inputs, such as minus 100 and minus 1000, while the steep middle gives very different outputs for two nearly equal inputs on either side of zero.

title: Training results: chance, overlap and repeated runs
facts_to_cover: Chance: Accuracy starts at **20 percent**, because with random weights the network knows nothing, and a random guess among **five** vowels is right one time in five.
Other counts: With ten categories, chance would be 10 percent.
Epoch: Each pass of learning is an **epoch**, and a problem like this takes thousands of them.
Leveling off: The network jumps to about 40 percent and levels off near **45 percent**, because the real vowel data **overlap** so much.
Overlap: Peterson and Barney found this overlap in the early 1950s. Even a person would have to guess for a point in the middle of the overlap.
Repeated runs: Ten runs from different random starting weights take **different paths but end at the same accuracy**, like children who hear different input but learn the same language.
Memorizing: Children first say went correctly by memory, then say goed after learning the pattern, then learn the exception (Carol Chomsky).

current_blocks.main: **The vowel network is trained on recordings of real speakers, and when their F1 and F2 are plotted, the vowels overlap.** Each dot is one recording, so one pair of formants does not always point to one vowel.
current_blocks.sub: Recordings with nearly the same F1 and F2 can be different vowels, so the network cannot find a separate patch for every vowel.
current_blocks.end: The accuracy you see is on the training data. Testing on new speakers is a separate question.

current_blocks.main: **Accuracy is how often the network picks the right word.** With five vowels, guessing at random is right one time in five, which is 20 percent.
current_blocks.sub: Accuracy rises as the weights learn and then levels off, which means more training is no longer helping.
current_blocks.end: The vowel network levels off near 45 percent on its training data, because the vowels overlap.

current_blocks.main: **Different random starting weights give different learning paths on the same data.**
current_blocks.sub: Ten runs that started from different random weights took different paths but ended at the same accuracy.
current_blocks.end: Running it many times gives better evidence than one run, because one run could be unusual.

questions.q: Why does accuracy start at 20 percent?
questions.a: There are five categories, and with random weights the network knows nothing, so its guesses are no better than chance. Guessing at random among five vowels is right one time in five, which is 20 percent.

questions.q: Why does accuracy start at 10 percent for a network with ten output categories?
questions.a: With random weights the network's guesses are no better than chance, and a random guess among ten categories is right one time in ten, which is 10 percent.

questions.q: Why does the vowel network level off near 40 to 45 percent instead of 100 percent?
questions.a: The real formant data for the five vowels overlap a great deal, so many recordings with nearly the same F1 and F2 belong to different vowels. For a point in the middle of the overlap, even a person would have to guess, so no network can classify those points reliably.

questions.q: Ten training runs start from different random weights. What happens?
questions.a: The runs take different paths, with some jumping up early and some staying at chance longer, but all of them end at about the same accuracy. Stochastic gradient descent involves chance along the way, but the end point is the same.

title: Leading up to LLMs: from one neuron to networks that unfold over time
facts_to_cover: All-or-none: The first paper on artificial neural networks, by McCulloch and Pitts, started from the all-or-none behavior of real neurons. A neuron is either firing or not firing, which is the same idea as the **sigmoid**.
From biology: The earliest neural network work tried to model how the mind works, including mental illness, so the field began in biology rather than in technology.

Parallel Distributed Processing: **Parallel** means many neurons calculate their activations at the same time. **Distributed** means the information from the inputs is spread across all the neurons. By the time of these books, forward propagation and backpropagation were well worked out.
Neuron: A neuron takes in a vector and gives back one number. It multiplies each input by its weight and adds the results, which is the **inner product**.
Neural network: A neural network repeats the inner product layer after layer. It takes in one vector and gives back a vector of decisions.

The limit: The vowel network takes one **static** vector, a fixed list of numbers from one moment, and makes one decision. Speech changes all the time and a sentence is many words one after another, so one fixed list of numbers cannot model thinking that unfolds over time.

title: Heads and layers
facts_to_cover: Layer: A layer is one round of improvement. Layers go one after another, from the input to the output.
Head: A head is one expert, and it is a set of weights. Heads sit side by side inside each layer.

What a layer does: Each head gives its own opinion on how to improve the vectors, and the layer combines all of the heads' opinions into improved vectors. The next layer then does the same thing again.
Classroom comparison: The classes you visit one after another are the layers, and the students in each class who each give you an opinion are the heads.
Depth and width: Layers give an LLM depth, one round of improvement after another. Heads give it width, many experts asked at the same time in each round.
Why so many: Predicting the next word is so hard that large systems have a hundred or more layers with about a hundred heads in each.
How heads learn: If the predicted next word is wrong, every head in every layer adjusts its weights with backpropagation, so the next prediction is closer to the right word.

title: Gestalt completion and the cloze test
facts_to_cover: Gestalt completion: Gestalt psychology studies how people see whole patterns. People see a triangle in the Gestalt figure even though no triangle is drawn, because a large part of human knowledge is completing what is missing.
Closure: Closure is the Gestalt word for completing a familiar pattern that is not quite finished, such as seeing a broken circle as whole.
Cloze test: Words are removed from a text and people fill them in. The name comes from closure, and it tests knowledge by asking someone to complete a sequence.
LLM learning: An LLM predicting the next word is playing a cloze game again and again. Training a system only to predict the missing piece turns out to copy human thinking.

title: Agentic systems and Software 3.0
facts_to_cover: Agentic system: An agentic system is a group of LLMs connected so that one's output becomes the next one's input. An agent in AI today is just an LLM.

The lecture example: An outline LLM plans the answer, a writing LLM writes it, a critic LLM checks it, a revision LLM works back and forth with the critic, and a final LLM produces the answer the user sees.

Shared memory and fixed weights: Once each LLM is trained its weights usually do not change, and the agents share a common memory where they write and read information.

Software 1.0, 2.0 and 3.0: Software 1.0 is writing a program in a language such as Python. Software 2.0 is training a neural network on input and output data, so the program is its weights. title: Phonotactics and guessing the next letter
facts_to_cover: Phonotactics: The rules for which sounds can follow which are **phonotactics**. Every speaker knows them without being taught.
Simple syllable: A simple English syllable is a consonant, a vowel and a consonant, as in Don or cup. The pattern is about sounds, not letters, so the silent e of shave does not count.

Onset and coda: A cluster before the vowel is an onset, as in split, and a cluster after the vowel is a coda, as in lamp. The order is a mirror image around the vowel, so flat is a word and lfat is impossible.

Syllable breaks: Atlantic is a word because t and l are on opposite sides of a syllable break, but tlantic is impossible because tl cannot start an English syllable. The sound ng can end a syllable but never start one.

Other languages: Mandarin allows only nasal sounds at the end of a syllable, Russian and Polish allow clusters like zb or dl at the start of a word, and Spanish speakers add an e before st, as in estadio.

Next-letter guessing: After a vowel, almost any letter can come next, so the probability distribution is flat. At the start of a word, the choices narrow to what an English onset allows, so after skr the distribution is sharply peaked on a few vowels.
The GPT link: Guessing the next letter is predicting the sixteenth item, so a GPT trained only on this game learns English syllable structure.

Allowed codas (after the vowel): desk, help, milk and lamp.

After sh_: Only a vowel or r can come next, as in shrimp.
